nodes.title: How should I structure the 60-minute technical interview?
nodes.summary: 60-minute slot to walk through the Branching Discussion Workspace project. Goal: give a clear, technical walkthrough of the three anchor flows while leaving 18 minutes for real discussion. Main constraint: balancing depth with pacing across 42 minutes of presentation.

nodes.title: How do I open the session and set the right lens?
nodes.summary: The opening needs to set expectations quickly: this is a technical deep-dive, not a product pitch. Frame around three end-to-end flows and signal that the discussion slot is real.
nodes.conclusion: Open by stating the three-flow structure upfront and inviting the interviewer to redirect at any point. Avoid product pitch language.
nodes.rationale: Interviewers calibrate quickly. Framing the structure upfront gives them a map and signals organized thinking from the first sentence.

nodes.title: Architecture Overview — three-package mental model
nodes.summary: React frontend, Express/tRPC backend, shared contracts package. Each owns a different layer of correctness: frontend owns interaction state, backend owns workflow correctness, shared keeps the contract honest. Keep this verbal and under 6 minutes.
nodes.conclusion: Verbal description only, no file navigation. Save code references for the flows where code confirms something the interviewer already understands conceptually.
nodes.rationale: Opening the file tree during architecture forces the interviewer to build a mental model of folder locations before understanding what the files do — overhead before the main content.

nodes.title: Flow 1 — App load → workspace tree → node conversation
nodes.summary: Simplest end-to-end path: auth → workspace list → Redux state → flat node fetch → tree hydration → fold overlay → layout → node selection → messages. Good warmup because it shows data pipeline discipline without async complexity.
nodes.conclusion: Narrate as a chain where each step names which layer owns that data and why. End by opening a node conversation to bridge into Flow 2.
nodes.rationale: Starting simple eases the interviewer into the data model. Key insight to land: backend returns flat rows, frontend owns tree hydration and layout.

nodes.title: Flow 2 — Send message → turn orchestration → SSE stream → persisted assistant message
nodes.summary: Strongest technical section. Covers idempotent turn creation, staged context prep, retrieval, generation, assistant persistence, stream event publishing, and SSE replay. 12 minutes. Key risk: too much pipeline detail kills pacing.

nodes.title: Flow 3 — Select assistant text → branch → bootstrap child conversation
nodes.summary: Most product-differentiated flow. Creates durable provenance: branch node, branch annotation, branch_event message in child. The UI overlay bridges the async gap between branch creation and turn completion.
nodes.conclusion: Frame as: 'A branch is a durable, explainable object in the data model — not just a UI redirect to a new chat panel.'
nodes.rationale: This is the core product differentiator. It needs to land as a system design decision, not a feature description.

nodes.title: Quality bar — tests, CI, and architectural guardrails
nodes.summary: Shared schemas as contract enforcement, flow tests around the turn pipeline and branch behavior, central test script, CI on PRs, ownership/query-layer boundary test. Signals engineering discipline without overclaiming coverage.

nodes.title: How do I explain the idempotency key simply?
nodes.summary: Lead with the failure mode, not the mechanism: a retry or double-tap creates duplicate messages without idempotency. The client generates a key before the call; the server returns the existing turn if the key has already been seen.
nodes.conclusion: Don't open with the word 'idempotency'. Describe the invariant plainly: submitted once, executed once, even if the network delivered it twice. Let the interviewer name the pattern if they recognize it.
nodes.rationale: Interviewers who know the term will confirm it from the description. Those who don't will follow the plain-language version without getting lost on vocabulary.

nodes.title: Why SSE over WebSockets — how do I answer this cleanly?
nodes.summary: SSE is unidirectional by design — right shape for token streaming. Browser-native with automatic reconnect. Replay model pairs naturally with persisted events. WebSockets add complexity without benefit for a one-directional stream.
nodes.conclusion: End the answer by naming the conditions under which WebSockets would be right. That signals SSE was deliberate, not a default.
nodes.rationale: This question will come up. A confident answer that acknowledges the tradeoff is stronger than one that defends SSE unconditionally.

nodes.title: Why is branch provenance stored as an event message rather than a FK?
nodes.summary: A FK on the child node records origin but is invisible in the conversation timeline. A branch_event message makes the branch origin part of the conversation itself — renderable, queryable, and part of the timeline rather than metadata sitting outside it.

messages.content: I have a 60-minute interview slot to walk through this project. I want to anchor the session around three concrete flows: app load to workspace tree, send message to SSE stream, and select assistant text to branch creation. Help me think through the overall structure so it feels cohesive rather than a feature checklist.

The three flows you've chosen are well-scoped. Each shows a different category of thinking: Flow 1 demonstrates frontend data pipeline discipline, Flow 2 shows backend workflow design under real async constraints, and Flow 3 combines both with product differentiation on top. They build from simpler to more complex, which means the interviewer's mental model grows incrementally.

Here's a structure for 42 minutes of presentation:

**0:00–0:03 — Opening.** Set the lens: technical deep-dive, not a product pitch. State the three flows upfront.

**0:03–0:08 — Problem and MVP scope.** Why this product exists, what you optimized for, what was deliberately deferred.

**0:08–0:14 — Architecture overview.** Three-package mental model — keep it verbal, no file navigation yet.

**0:14–0:21 — Flow 1.** Simplest path first. End by opening a node conversation to bridge into Flow 2.

**0:21–0:33 — Flow 2.** Your strongest technical section. Go slower here. Don't cover every pipeline stage — pick three decisions that each illustrate a different design tradeoff.

**0:33–0:40 — Flow 3.** Most product-specific. Frame branching as a data model decision, not a UI interaction.

**0:40–0:45 — Quality and guardrails.**

**0:45–1:00 — Open discussion.**

One calibration: in Flow 2, resist the urge to walk through every pipeline stage. Idempotency, staged persistence, and SSE replay together tell the real design story — those three anchors are enough.
Good structure. My concern is that 42 minutes of presentation risks becoming a monologue. How do I keep it feeling like a technical conversation rather than a rehearsed script?

A few techniques that work well in technical walkthroughs:

**Surface the decision, not just the outcome.** At each interesting design point, briefly name the alternative you considered: *'I could have used WebSockets here, but chose SSE because...'* Interviewers engage immediately when they see you've actually reasoned through a tradeoff.

**Use checkpoint questions.** After each flow: *'Does that land, or would it help to slow down on any stage?'* This gives them a natural entry point and shows you're paying attention to their comprehension.

**Offer a branch mid-session.** Around the 25-minute mark: *'I've covered the load path and the turn lifecycle — would you like to go deeper on the streaming layer, or move to the branching flow?'* That makes it feel like a dialogue.

**In code sections, point at one function per stage.** Read one or two lines that carry the key invariant, explain why that invariant matters, and move on. Interviewers are pattern-matching for how you think, not checking every line.
Help me write the actual opening sentences I'll say out loud. I want to set the right technical tone in the first 30 seconds without sounding like I rehearsed from a script.

Here's a version you can adapt:

> *'I'll keep this focused on three things: the product idea at a high level, the architecture that supports it, and then three concrete user flows from frontend interaction to backend orchestration to persisted state. I built this to work through problems that don't come up in tutorial apps — async workflows, branching state, streaming, full-stack contracts. Happy to go deeper on any part as we go.'*

What makes this work: it sets the structure immediately so the interviewer has a map, it names what you optimized for rather than what you built, and the last sentence signals the discussion time is real — not courtesy minutes at the end.

One thing to avoid: starting with *'So this is a full-stack project where...'* That construction signals you're describing rather than presenting. The version above assumes the interviewer is already in the room with you.
How do I explain the three-package split — React frontend, Express/tRPC backend, shared contracts — in a way that sounds like a deliberate design decision rather than just describing a monorepo?

The frame that works: **each package owns a different layer of correctness.**

> *'The frontend owns interaction state — fold state, selection state, optimistic messages, local draft. The backend owns workflow correctness — turn ordering, persistence guarantees, event publishing. The shared package keeps the contract honest — router schemas, metadata types, enums that both sides depend on.'*

That framing makes the split feel intentional rather than organizational. It also leads to a natural follow-up: when something goes wrong, you know which layer is responsible. A UI state bug is frontend. A persistence race is backend. A shape mismatch between them is a shared schema issue — and that's exactly the class of problem tRPC with shared schemas catches at compile time rather than runtime.

If they ask why tRPC instead of REST: *'tRPC gives you a typed contract without a code generation step. In a monorepo where I'm working across both sides, if I change a procedure signature the TypeScript error appears in the component that calls it before I even run the server.'*
Should I pull up actual code during the architecture section, or keep this part verbal?

Keep it verbal here. The architecture section is about giving the interviewer a map, not showing them territory. If you open the file tree now, you're forcing them to build a mental model of file locations before they understand what the files do — overhead you don't need before the flows.

Save code references for the flows, where you can say: *'This is the exact function where this decision is enforced'* and the code confirms something they already understand conceptually.

One exception: if they ask directly — *'Can you show me how the shared schema is consumed?'* — pull it up immediately. But don't volunteer code during the architecture section.
Help me narrate Flow 1 in a way that sets up Flow 2 rather than just being an inventory of what the frontend does.

The narrative hook for Flow 1 is: **the backend returns flat rows, and the frontend does the interesting work.**

Here's a narration shape that builds toward Flow 2:

> *'Once auth is established, the client fetches the flat node list for the active workspace — that's a simple DB query, the backend just returns rows. The interesting part is what the frontend does with them: it hydrates those flat rows into a nested tree, overlays local fold state from Redux, and computes a render layout. None of that is server state — it's interaction state the frontend owns entirely.*

> *Clicking a node opens the conversation panel and fires a second query: messages scoped to that node. Scoped to the node — not the whole workspace — which matters a lot once you have a branched tree where each node has its own conversation thread.*

> *That scoping is the bridge to Flow 2: when you send a message in this panel, the turn lifecycle begins.'*

You've introduced flat-to-tree hydration, the local/server state split, and node-scoped messaging — all load-bearing for Flows 2 and 3.

This is my most complex section and I have 12 minutes. There are probably 8 distinct stages in the turn pipeline. Help me decide which three design decisions to highlight so I'm not just walking through a list.

The three decisions that tell the real design story:

**1. Idempotency before the pipeline starts.** Before any work begins, the server checks whether this turn already exists using a client-generated key. This is the first signal that you're treating this as a workflow with replay semantics, not a request that happens to return text. If the key exists, the server returns the existing turn — no duplicate messages, no duplicate generation.

**2. User message persistence is separated from assistant persistence.** The user message is written to the DB first, before context prep or generation. This means the user's message is durable even if generation fails. The assistant message is written only after successful generation. Staged persistence — the UI's pending state reflects real server state, not just optimistic local state.

**3. Stream events are both persisted and broker-published.** Token deltas and status transitions are written to an event store *and* published to a live broker. This is why SSE replay works: on reconnect, the route replays persisted events first, then switches to live. Without persistence, a reconnect during generation would lose all tokens already streamed.

Those three together show replay thinking, staged persistence, and the separation of durable state from real-time delivery. That's the design story in 12 minutes.
I keep stumbling when I get to the idempotency part. Interviewers sometimes look confused. Is there a cleaner way to introduce it without assuming they know the term?

The stumbling usually comes from explaining the mechanism before the problem. Lead with the failure mode instead:

> *'The naive implementation sends a request and waits. If the network hiccups, the user retries. Now you have two user messages and two assistant turns from one submitted message. Idempotency prevents that: the client generates a key before the call. If the same key arrives twice — retry, double-tap, or network blip — the server returns the already-created turn instead of starting a new one.'*

That version is self-contained. They don't need to know the word going in — you've described the problem, the mechanism, and the outcome in three sentences. Interviewers who know the term will name it themselves, which is a better outcome than you defining it.

This is worth branching into its own node so we can work through the exact wording until it's natural to say out loud.

The branching feature is what makes this project distinctive, but I keep explaining it in a way that sounds like 'I added a button that opens a new chat panel.' How do I make sure it lands as a system design decision?

The framing that works: **a branch is a durable event in the data model, not a navigation action in the UI.**

Here's how to set that up:

> *'When a user selects a span of assistant text and branches, three things are created transactionally: a child node in the tree, a branch annotation that records the exact text selection and message origin, and a branch_event message in the child node's conversation that makes the branch origin visible in the conversation timeline — not just as metadata on the node.*

> *That means the branch is explainable: you can always answer "where did this branch come from?" by reading the child's first message. You can render it, query it, link back to the source. It's a first-class object in the data model.'*

The contrast to draw: most implementations that do 'branching' create a new conversation with the parent ID in a column. What makes this different is that the branch origin is captured as a timeline event — part of the conversation itself, not a record reference sitting outside it.

One specific thing I struggle to explain: why is branch provenance stored as an event message in the child conversation rather than just a foreign key on the child node? I want to be able to answer that tradeoff clearly if someone pushes on it.

Good one to branch — the tradeoff is specific enough that rushing a quick answer here will produce a vague answer. The short version: a FK tells you where the branch came from, but a message in the conversation timeline makes the branch origin *part of the conversation itself*, which changes what you can do with it at the UI layer.

Let's work through the exact comparison in the branch so you have a crisp answer ready.
How much time should I spend on tests and CI? I don't want to oversell it since coverage isn't exhaustive, but I also don't want it to feel like an afterthought.

Two minutes is the right length. The goal is to show you turned architectural intentions into automated checks rather than just conventions and comments — not to claim exhaustive coverage.

A framing that works:

> *'I focused tests around two areas: the turn pipeline, because getting that flow wrong has cascading effects on persistence and streaming, and the ownership boundary, because I wanted to enforce that query logic stays in one layer rather than drifting into route handlers. I also set up a central test script and CI so that "the tests pass" means something consistent rather than something you have to remember to check.'*

That does three things: it explains *why* those areas have tests (not just that they do), it shows you thought about where bugs would hurt most, and it names the ownership boundary test specifically — which is the most architectural thing in the suite and the most interesting to discuss if they follow up.

Branched from: [Flow 2 — Send message → turn orchestration → SSE stream] — assistant response identifying the three key design decisions to highlight. Branched to refine the idempotency explanation until it feels natural to say out loud.
Give me a polished one-paragraph explanation of why I added idempotency to the turn flow, written for someone who hasn't built a chat system before. I want to be able to say this verbatim.

Here's a version you can say verbatim:

> *'When you submit a message, there's a window where the request is in-flight but you don't have confirmation yet. If the user taps again, the browser retries, or the network drops and reconnects, you can end up with the same message submitted twice — which means two user messages and two AI turns from a single action. To prevent that, the client generates a unique key before making the request. The server checks that key first: if it's already seen it, it returns the existing turn rather than starting a new one. The user's action is still atomic from their perspective — they submitted once — even if the network tried to deliver it more than once.'*

Practice saying this once or twice. The word 'idempotency' doesn't appear — you've described the invariant in plain language. If the interviewer wants the term, they'll name it themselves, which signals they understood the concept and are confirming the vocabulary rather than needing you to define it.

Branched from: [Flow 2 — Send message → turn orchestration → SSE stream] — architecture overview discussion on streaming transport. The SSE vs WebSockets question is likely to come up — preparing a crisp, honest answer.
Give me a 3–4 sentence answer for 'Why SSE over WebSockets?' that's honest about the tradeoff rather than sounding defensive.

Here's a version that's confident and honest:

> *'SSE is unidirectional by design — the server streams to the client, and the client sends back through the existing tRPC HTTP channel. For token streaming, that's exactly the shape of the problem: I don't need the client to push data over the stream, so a bidirectional channel adds complexity without adding capability. SSE is also browser-native with automatic reconnect, which pairs well with the event replay model — on reconnect, the server replays persisted events from the turn's beginning so no tokens are lost. WebSockets would make sense if I needed low-latency client-to-server messages over the same channel, or real-time multi-user sync — neither is true for this MVP.'*

The key move is ending with the conditions under which WebSockets would be right. That tells the interviewer SSE was deliberate, not a default.

Branched from: [Flow 3 — Select assistant text → branch → bootstrap child conversation] — question about why branch provenance is stored as an event message rather than a FK on the child node. Exploring the exact tradeoff.
Walk me through the actual practical difference between a FK on the child node versus a branch_event message in the conversation timeline. What can you do with one that you can't do with the other?

The FK approach — `child_node.branched_from_message_id` — gives you the origin reference. You can look up where the branch came from. That's useful, and for many use cases it's sufficient.

But it has two limitations:

**It's invisible in the conversation timeline.** The conversation panel shows messages in order. A FK on the node record doesn't appear there — so when a user opens the child node, they see a conversation that starts from nothing. There's no visible anchor to the parent context.

**It can't carry narrative content.** A FK is a pointer. A branch_event message is a message — it can render in the timeline with a quote of the selected text, a link back to the source, a timestamp, and context about what triggered the branch. It becomes part of the conversation's own history rather than metadata outside it.

The tradeoff is that a message is heavier than a FK — a row in the messages table versus two columns on the node. But for this use case the heaviness is the point: the branch event *should* be a first-class thing in the conversation, because the branch is a first-class thing in the product.

One-line version if you need it: *'I wanted the branch origin to be part of the conversation, not metadata about the conversation.'*
Give me a quick day-of cheat sheet — the key lines and framing I should have ready before I walk in.

**Opening line**
- *'I'll walk through three end-to-end flows — app load, message turn lifecycle, and branching — then open it up for discussion.'*

**Architecture one-liner**
- Frontend owns interaction state, backend owns workflow correctness, shared package keeps the contract honest.

**Flow 2 — three anchors to hit**
- Idempotency: client generates a key; server returns the existing turn on a duplicate, so submitted-once means executed-once
- Staged persistence: user message is written first, before generation; assistant message written only after success
- SSE replay: events are both persisted and broker-published, so a reconnect replays from the beginning of the turn

**Flow 3 — the one framing that has to land**
- *'A branch is a durable, explainable object in the data model — not a UI redirect to a new chat panel.'*
- Three things created transactionally: child node, branch annotation, branch_event message in the child's timeline

**Tradeoff answers**
- Why SSE over WebSockets: unidirectional is the right shape; replay is first-class; WebSockets if you need bidirectional or multi-user sync
- Why tRPC: typed contract without codegen; shape mismatches surface at compile time in the component that calls the procedure
- Biggest non-production shortcuts: in-memory sessions, localhost CORS, assistant echo-debug mode, auth hardening deferred

**Closing line if they ask what you'd improve next**
- *'Remove the echo override, productionize auth/session storage, and finish the merge-back proof loop — the branching half is built, the parent-resume path is the next design problem.'*
